title: Pastoral Care and Counselling
summary: How to care for God's people biblically and wisely: the shepherd's heart, listening and counselling skills, ministry in grief, sickness and crisis, and knowing when to refer.
description: "Feed the flock of God which is among you" (1 Peter 5:2). This course equips pastors, elders, deacons and caring church members to shepherd people through life's struggles. It covers the biblical basis of care, the skills of listening and biblical counselling, care for the sick, dying and bereaved, help in marriage and family conflict, depression and anxiety, and the boundaries, confidentiality and referral that keep care safe.
objectives: Explain the biblical basis and goal of pastoral care
Practise listening and biblical counselling skills
Care for the sick, the dying and the bereaved
Help people facing conflict, depression, anxiety and crisis
Practise safe boundaries, confidentiality and referral
outcomes: Describe the shepherd's work from Ezekiel 34 and John 10
Use active listening and good questions
Lead a hospital visit and support a grieving family
Recognise signs that require professional help
Apply confidentiality and its limits wisely

modules.title: The Shepherd's Heart
modules.intro: Pastoral care is shepherding God's flock as Christ does. This week we study its biblical foundation.

lessons.title: The Good Shepherd
lessons.body:
"The LORD is my shepherd" (Psalm 23:1). God promised, "I will feed my flock... I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick" (Ezekiel 34:15-16).

Jesus is "the good shepherd" who "giveth his life for the sheep" and knows them by name (John 10:11, 14). He was "moved with compassion" for the crowds, "as sheep having no shepherd" (Matthew 9:36).

All pastoral care flows from His care. We are under-shepherds of "the chief Shepherd" (1 Peter 5:4).

lessons.title: Bad shepherds and good shepherds
lessons.body:
God condemned Israel's leaders: "Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves!... The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick... but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them" (Ezekiel 34:2-4).

Good shepherds:

- **Know** the flock: "Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks" (Proverbs 27:23).
- **Feed** them with the Word.
- **Lead** by example.
- **Protect** them from wolves (Acts 20:28-29).
- **Seek** the straying (Luke 15:4).
- **Heal** and bind up the broken.

Care is not only the pastor's job: believers are to "bear one another's burdens" (Galatians 6:2).

lessons.title: The goal of care
lessons.body:
The goal of pastoral care is not merely to solve problems or make people feel better, but to help them know God and grow in Christ through their circumstances: "that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus" (Colossians 1:28).

God comforts us "that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God" (2 Corinthians 1:4).

Care involves the whole person: spiritual, emotional, physical and practical. Sometimes the most spiritual thing to do is bring food, pay a hospital bill, or sit in silence. Job's friends did best in the first seven days, when they sat with him and said nothing (Job 2:13).

A church leader who shepherds under Christ the chief Shepherd.
One who feeds, leads, protects and heals the flock.
Deep pity that moves to help.
Caring by being with someone in their suffering.
Caring for spiritual, emotional, physical and practical needs.

Care aims at Christlikeness and meets the whole person's needs.

modules.title: Listening and Counselling
modules.intro: Counselling begins with listening. This week we study the skills and process of biblical counselling.

lessons.title: Swift to hear
lessons.body:
"Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (James 1:19). "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" (Proverbs 18:13).

**Active listening** means:

- Giving full attention: put the phone away, look at the person.
- Not interrupting or jumping to advice.
- Reflecting back: "It sounds like you feel..."
- Asking open questions: "How did that affect you?" "What have you tried?"
- Listening for feelings as well as facts.

"Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out" (Proverbs 20:5).

lessons.title: Biblical counselling
lessons.body:
Scripture is "profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness" (2 Timothy 3:16). Biblical counselling brings God's Word to bear on people's struggles with wisdom and love.

A simple process:

1. **Listen and understand** the person and situation.
2. **Discern** what is happening in the heart: fears, desires, beliefs, sin and suffering (Proverbs 4:23; Jeremiah 17:9).
3. **Bring Scripture**: God's character, promises and commands that speak to the situation.
4. **Call to response**: repentance, faith, forgiveness, obedience, or lament and trust.
5. **Plan practical steps** and follow up.

"Speaking the truth in love" (Ephesians 4:15).

lessons.title: Suffering and sin
lessons.body:
People come with both **suffering** (things done to them, loss, illness) and **sin** (their own wrong responses or choices). Often both are present.

We must distinguish: blaming sufferers for their pain, like Job's friends, is cruel (Job 42:7). Yet ignoring sin leaves people trapped.

Paul's guidance: "warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men" (1 Thessalonians 5:14). Different people need different responses.

Never counsel with a hidden agenda, manipulation or harshness. Pray with and for those you counsel, and depend on the Spirit, "the Comforter" (John 14:16).

terms.def: Listening with full attention, reflecting back and asking open questions.
Restating what a person has said to show understanding.
Bringing Scripture to bear on people's struggles with wisdom and love.
In Scripture, the centre of a person's desires, thoughts and choices.
Honest grief expressed to God in faith.
Honest counsel given with genuine care (Ephesians 4:15).

Answering before hearing is folly and shame.
A man of understanding draws out counsel from the heart.

modules.title: Care in Sickness, Death and Grief
modules.intro: Some of the most important care happens in hospitals and at gravesides. This week we study ministry to the sick, dying and bereaved.

lessons.title: Visiting the sick
lessons.body:
"I was sick, and ye visited me" (Matthew 25:36). James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14).

Guidelines for hospital and home visits:

- Keep visits short unless invited to stay.
- Respect hospital rules and the patient's privacy.
- Listen more than talk; do not compare with others' illnesses.
- Read a short, comforting passage such as Psalm 23, 46 or 121, and pray simply.
- Do not promise healing God has not promised, or blame illness on lack of faith.
- Offer practical help to the family: food, transport, help with bills.

Visit faithfully, especially those with long illnesses who are often forgotten.

lessons.title: Ministry to the dying
lessons.body:
Being with the dying is a sacred trust. Help them:

- Be sure of their salvation: share the gospel gently if needed, and assurance from John 14:1-3 and Romans 8:38-39.
- Make peace: forgiving and being forgiven, reconciling with family.
- Settle practical matters: a will and wishes for burial, to prevent family conflict.
- Face death with hope: "to die is gain" (Philippians 1:21).

Pray, sing familiar hymns, read Scripture, and simply be present. Support the family, who are also exhausted and grieving. "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints" (Psalm 116:15).

lessons.title: Comforting the bereaved
lessons.body:
"Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted" (Matthew 5:4). Jesus wept with Mary and Martha though He knew He would raise Lazarus (John 11:35).

Grief takes time and may include shock, sorrow, anger, guilt and loneliness. It is not lack of faith. Believers "sorrow not, even as others which have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13), but they do sorrow.

Help: be present; listen to memories; avoid clichés like "it is God's will" said too quickly; help with practical needs; protect widows from harmful customs and property grabbing (James 1:27); and keep visiting after the funeral, when others have gone. Anniversaries and holidays can be hard.

Spiritual and practical care for those near death and their families.
The loss of a loved one through death.

Help the dying find assurance, peace and hope.
Grief is normal; believers grieve with hope.

modules.title: Crisis, Conflict and Safe Care
modules.intro: This week we study care in conflict, depression, anxiety and crisis, and the boundaries that keep care safe.

lessons.title: Conflict and reconciliation
lessons.body:
Conflict arises in marriages, families and churches. "From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts?" (James 4:1).

In helping:

- Hear both sides before judging (Proverbs 18:17).
- Help each person examine their own heart first (Matthew 7:3-5).
- Encourage confession, forgiveness and practical change (Colossians 3:13).
- Use the steps of Matthew 18:15-17 where sin persists.

Where there is **abuse or violence**, safety comes first. Do not send a victim back into danger in the name of reconciliation. Involve appropriate authorities and professional help.

lessons.title: Depression, anxiety and crisis
lessons.body:
Godly people in Scripture knew deep distress: Elijah prayed to die (1 Kings 19:4); David cried, "Why art thou cast down, O my soul?" (Psalm 42:5); Paul despaired of life (2 Corinthians 1:8).

God cared for Elijah with rest, food, His presence and a new task (1 Kings 19:5-18). Depression and anxiety can have spiritual, emotional, physical and social causes, and are not simply a lack of faith.

Take **talk of suicide or self-harm** seriously: stay with the person, ask directly, help them get urgent medical help, and involve family. Encourage ongoing professional care alongside the church's support and prayer. "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee" (Psalm 55:22).

lessons.title: Boundaries, confidentiality and referral
lessons.body:
Safe care requires:

- **Confidentiality**: do not gossip about what is shared (Proverbs 11:13). But confidentiality has limits: when someone is at risk of harm, or a child is being abused, you must act and involve appropriate people and authorities.
- **Boundaries**: meet in suitable places; counsel the opposite sex with another person present or nearby; avoid emotional or physical entanglement; do not create dependence on yourself.
- **Referral**: know your limits. Refer to doctors, mental-health professionals, lawyers or social services when needed. Moses accepted Jethro's advice to share the load (Exodus 18:17-23).
- **Self-care**: carers need rest, support and their own walk with God (Mark 6:31).

terms.def: Restoring broken relationships through confession and forgiveness.

assignments.title: A care visit
assignments.prompt: Visit someone who is sick, elderly or bereaved (with their permission). Without naming them, describe how you listened, what Scripture you shared, how you prayed, what practical help was needed, and what you learned, using the course passages.

assignments.title: A church care plan
assignments.prompt: Write a pastoral care plan for your church covering visitation, care for the sick and bereaved, a response to crises such as suicide risk or abuse, confidentiality and its limits, and a list of local referral options.
